context.text: In the early seventh century the eastern empire fought for its life, first against Persia and then against the Arabs, and the division over Chalcedon ran through the very provinces it had to hold. Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, sought a formula that might reunite the churches: Christ has two natures, but a single operation, or energy. In 633 Cyrus of Alexandria made a union on these terms with many of the non-Chalcedonians of Egypt.

The first to protest was the monk Sophronius, soon patriarch of Jerusalem, whose synodal letter set out that each nature in Christ acts according to what it is. To quiet the dispute, Sergius began to speak instead of one will in Christ, and Pope Honorius of Rome, writing to him, used the same expression. In 638 the emperor Heraclius made it law in an edict called the Ekthesis; in 648 his grandson Constans II, finding the quarrel only worse, forbade anyone to speak of either one will or two.

The answer was carried by St Maximus the Confessor, a monk once in the imperial service. A nature without its own will, he argued, is not a real nature; if the Word did not take a human will, He did not become fully man, and what He did not take He did not heal. In Gethsemane the Lord's human will is seen, and seen obeying:
O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.

narrative.text: In 649 Pope Martin held a synod at the Lateran in Rome, with Maximus present, which condemned the one will and the emperor's edicts. The price was paid in full. Martin was arrested in 653, tried in Constantinople as a traitor, and died in exile at Cherson in the Crimea in 655. Maximus was tried more than once; in 662, refusing to the end to enter communion with those who confessed one will, he had his tongue and his right hand cut off, and died in exile in the Caucasus that summer.

Two decades later the emperor Constantine IV, wanting peace with Rome, asked for a council. Pope Agatho sent legates with a long letter setting out the faith of two wills, and the council met from November 680 to September 681 in the domed hall of the palace called the Trullus. The emperor attended many of the eighteen sessions in person. In the eighth, the bishops under Constantinople declared one by one that they accepted the pope's letter. Macarius, patriarch of Antioch, would not:
I do not say that there are two wills or two operations in the dispensation of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, but one will and one theandric operation.
narrative.source: Macarius of Antioch, Acts of the Sixth Council, Session VIII, tr. H. R. Percival (NPNF2 vol. 14, 1900)

narrative.text: Patristic texts brought in to support him were found to have been cut short or altered, and he was deposed. In its thirteenth session the council examined the letters of Sergius and Honorius, judged them contrary to the faith, and condemned the leaders of the one-will party by name, Honorius among them. The synodal letter of Sophronius it received as orthodox.

In the last session the bishops set out their Definition of Faith. It repeats Chalcedon and then adds that in Christ there are two natural wills and two natural operations, and it explains how they stand to one another:

And these two natural wills are not contrary the one to the other (God forbid!) as the impious heretics assert, but his human will follows and that not as resisting and reluctant, but rather as subject to his divine and omnipotent will.
narrative.source: The Definition of Faith of the Sixth Council, tr. H. R. Percival (NPNF2 vol. 14, 1900)

narrative.text: In their address to the emperor the bishops gave thanks for the pope's letter in words that have been remembered since: Peter spoke through Agatho.

significance.text: The council carried Chalcedon to its end. Christ took everything that belongs to our nature, a human will included, and freely joined it to the will of God; in Him human freedom is not abolished but healed. This is the ground of the Orthodox teaching that salvation is God's work in which we take part with our whole selves, and that obedience to God is not the loss of the will but its freedom.
It also vindicated the confessors. Maximus, who died mutilated and condemned, and Martin, who died a prisoner, had defended the faith the whole Church now proclaimed.

consequences.text: Neither the Fifth nor the Sixth Council had issued canons, and in 691 and 692 bishops met again in the same hall to supply them, in the council called in Trullo, whose canons the Orthodox Church counts with the Sixth. The one-will teaching was revived briefly under the emperor Philippicus in 712 and set aside again after his fall. The Church keeps the memory of St Maximus on 21 January and of St Martin in April.

uncertainty: How Honorius should be judged has been argued for centuries: some hold that he meant only that Christ had no will contrary to God's, and that his fault was carelessness rather than heresy; the council, and later popes who repeated its sentence, condemned him by name. The dates of Maximus's trials and exile are given variously in the sources.

people.name: St Maximus the Confessor
people.role: Monk and theologian who defended the two wills, mutilated and exiled in 662.

people.name: St Martin the Confessor
people.role: Pope of Rome, who held the Lateran synod of 649 and died a prisoner at Cherson in 655.

people.name: St Sophronius of Jerusalem
people.role: Patriarch of Jerusalem, the first to protest, whose synodal letter the council received.

people.name: St Agatho of Rome
people.role: Pope of Rome, whose letter on the two wills the council accepted.

people.name: Emperor Constantine IV
people.role: Emperor, who called the council and attended many of its sessions.

people.name: Macarius of Antioch
people.role: Patriarch of Antioch, who held to one will and was deposed by the council.

people.name: Sergius of Constantinople
people.role: Patriarch, who first proposed one operation and then one will in Christ.

people.name: Pope Honorius
people.role: Bishop of Rome, whose letter to Sergius spoke of one will, condemned by name by the council.
